candidates.title: Genetic and biochemical screens identify MGAT1 as a druggable glycosyltransferase target in STK11-mutant lung cancer
candidates.authors: Vassallo KM, Chen YnP, Handing KB, Lu AZ, Meier SR, Liu S, Shen B, Teng T, Yu Y, Ji L, Lazarides K, Huang A, Min C, Haines BB, Mallender WD, Sun S, Liu MS, Amor AJ, Whittington DA, Salerno R, Bruzzese FJ, Maxwell JP, Maynard A, McCarren P, Come JH, Throner S, Andersen JN, Zhang W, Gueroussov S
candidates.abstract: Checkpoint inhibitors are standard-of-care therapies for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but their efficacy is limited in tumors with STK11 mutations, highlighting the need for new therapeutic strategies. Here, we performed complementary in vivo and in vitro CRISPR-Cas9 functional genomic screens to identify genes whose loss restores sensitivity to anti-PD-1 therapy. We found that loss of MGAT1, a Golgi glycosyltransferase critical for the maturation of high-mannose N-glycans into hybrid and complex glycan structures, reversed resistance to anti-PD-1 treatment in syngeneic mouse tumor models harboring STK11 mutations. Parallel co-culture screens with antigen-matched CD8+ T cells further showed that disruption of N-glycosylation strongly sensitized tumor cells to T cell–mediated killing. Genetic rescue studies demonstrated that this immune-evasion phenotype depends on MGAT1 catalytic activity, supporting direct biochemical interrogation of the enzyme. Using purified human MGAT1 and a UDP-Glo glycosyltransferase assay, we established a tractable screening platform and performed a 500,000-compound biochemical high-throughput screen, identifying an initial hit (Compound 1; IC50 = 197 μM). Subsequent medicinal chemistry optimization delivered progressively more potent analogs, including TNG-9333 (0.814 μM) and TNG-2673 (0.043 μM) and represented a >1000-fold improvement in biochemical potency from the starting hit. Crystal structures of human MGAT1 in apo, UDP-bound, UDP-GlcNAc-bound, and inhibitor-bound states, together with SPR and DSF analyses, revealed that this chemical series engages a previously unrecognized allosteric pocket and inhibits MGAT1 through a UDP-noncompetitive mechanism. Collectively, our work implicates N-glycosylation as a key mediator of immune evasion and establishes MGAT1 as a ligandable, structurally tractable target for small-molecule drug discovery.

candidates.title: Highly effective viral RdRP translocation hindrance by the remdesivir nucleotide
candidates.authors: Li R, Shao Q, Wang M, Feng C, Xu Q, Wang Q, Shang L, Xu Y, Gong P
candidates.abstract: AbstractNucleoside/nucleotide analogs (NAs) typically interfere with substrate selection and catalysis steps of polymerase nucleotide addition cycle (NAC), thereby affecting polymerase catalytic efficiency. In contrast, their interference with post-chemistry translocation is rarely considered in rational design, partly due to a lack of direct and quantitative evidence for such interference. Remdesivir (RDV) is an adenosine analog with broad-spectrum antiviral activity against diverse RNA virus families and has been approved for COVID-19 treatment. RDV is capable of inducing a characteristic “delayed” intervention, wherein the interference occurs several NACs after its incorporation. By combining X-ray crystallography, quench-flow kinetics, and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that the composite rate of RDV translocation from product strand position −3 to −4 and subsequent catalysis is at least 100-fold slower than that of adenosine in an enterovirus RdRP. However, mutating the corresponding roadblock residue serine417 to glycine largely abolishes this difference. Nonetheless, the incorporated RDV nucleotide can still alter the free-energy landscape even in the S417G mutant complex, enabling the capture of an over-translocated state. Our work demonstrates translocation-related intervention as an effective and broadly applicable polymerase intervention strategy in NA rational design.

candidates.title: Stk1 is required for BlaR1-mediated broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance in epidemic-causing strains of Staphylococcus aureus
candidates.authors: Poon R, Satishkumar N, Mosimann WA, Hayatnagarkar VD, Bose S, Hemmadi V, Kuhn S, Chatterjee A, Worrall L, Manes NP, Alexander JAN, Lack J, Chambers HF, Nita-Lazar A, Strynadka NCJ, Chatterjee SS
candidates.abstract: Sensory induction of mecA expression plays a pivotal role in mediating broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance of MRSA. In contemporary MRSA isolates, sensory induction of β-lactam resistance originates at the membrane-associated BlaR1, which, upon detection of β-lactam drugs, triggers a signal transduction cascade that promotes mecA induction. We hereby show that phosphorylation of BlaR1, mediated through the serine-threonine kinase, Stk1, stabilizes its membrane-spanning state and retention, allowing for proper drug sensing and subsequent signal transduction events to occur, culminating in mecA-mediated β-lactam resistance. Our results demonstrate that targeting Stk1 can potentiate synthetic lethality to β-lactams in the majority of naturally isolated strains of MRSA. We additionally present the structural and kinetic basis for a Stk1-inhibitor complex that can enable rational design of Stk1-directed anti-MRSA therapeutics in the future. Our results reveal a novel role of the STK signaling pathway in bacterial protein stabilization in the cytosolic membrane.

candidates.title: Structure and mechanism of inhibition of lysine demethylase 2A (KDM2A) by compound 183c
candidates.authors: Mader P, Liu L, Vallée F, Denis F, Pau V, Mao D, Caldwell L, Chan K, Kurinov I, Mamane Y, Parikh P, Zhang Z, Gallant M, Tyers M, Black WC, Zinda M, Durocher D, Wrana J, Zimmermann M, Sicheri F
candidates.abstract: Lysine demethylase 2A (KDM2A) is a key epigenetic regulator and promising target for inhibition since its loss is selectively lethal in cancers reliant on Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres (ALT). Here we investigated the mechanism of compound 183c, a potent KDM2A inhibitor described in the patent literature. Biophysical studies showed that 183c requires the co-factor 2-oxoglutarate (2OG) for binding. A 2.2 Å crystal structure of the KDM2A–183c–2OG ternary complex explained the selectivity of 183c and revealed how 183c occupies the H3K36me2 substrate pocket, with a crucial group mimicking dimethylated lysine 36. In proliferation assays, several ALT-positive cell lines were selectively sensitive to 183c. Comparing ALT-positive SAOS2 and ALT-negative SJSA1 cells, both showed repression of E2F-regulated genes, but only SJSA1 activated EMT, DNA repair, and mTOR pathways, indicating distinct adaptive responses. These structural and cellular insights establish a foundation for designing improved KDM2A inhibitors for ALT-positive cancers.

candidates.title: Mechanism of M18BP1-mediated activation of condensin II for mitotic DNA compaction
candidates.authors: Borsellini A, Chamera S, Cecatiello V, Andrecka J, Vannini A
candidates.abstract: AbstractDNA compaction by human condensin II is crucial for the correct organization of mitotic chromosomes. Mitotic activation of condensin II is a multilayered process, controlled mainly by the opposing activity of the MCPH1 and M18BP1 proteins, acting as an interphase inhibitor and a mitotic activator, respectively. Mitotic phosphorylation favors M18BP1 binding to condensin II, resulting in effective and timely chromosome compaction. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying condensin II activation in driving DNA compaction remain uncharacterized. Here, combining cryo-electron microscopy with single-molecule imaging, we unravel the mechanism of condensin II activation by M18BP1 and elucidate their role in DNA compaction. The specific interaction with phosphorylated M18BP1 induces conformational changes in the condensin II complex, relieving an autoinhibitory conformation and allowing stable DNA binding and DNA compaction. Beyond the activity of isolated condensin II complexes on DNA, we observe the emergence of multimeric species that withstand the forces applied by optical tweezers, suggesting that condensin II multimerization might contribute to the mechanical reinforcement of mitotic chromosomes.

candidates.title: Structure based discovery of antipsychotic-like TAAR1 agonists
candidates.authors: Huang S, Liu H, Wu Y, Braz JM, Kranthi D, Hall BW, Zhang X, Radchenko DS, Moroz YS, Irwin JJ, Basbaum AI, Xu HE, Wetsel WC, Shoichet BK
candidates.abstract: Schizophrenia is a severe mental illness whose current treatments primarily target dopamine and serotonin receptors. These drugs often cause side effects and vary in effectiveness across patients. The trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1), which modulates monoamine signaling, has emerged as a promising alternative target. To discover previously unexplored TAAR1 ligands, we computationally dock 65 million molecules against the active state of TAAR1 and experimentally test 55 of those highly ranked. Fourteen TAAR1 agonists emerge with potencies ranging from mid-nanomolar to micromolar. This high functional selectivity may reflect the compact conformation adopted by the activated TAAR1 orthosteric site. While this is favorable for agonist prioritization, simulations suggest that it can be over-optimized for initial hit rates at the expense of subsequent affinity maturation. Hit optimization yields nanomolar agonists whose docking-predicted poses are confirmed by cryo-EM. Three agonists have high brain exposure and potencies, with one compound showing potency comparable to the investigational drug ulotaront and two compounds exhibiting even greater potency, at levels sufficient for behavioral studies. All three potently normalize amphetamine-induced pre-pulse inhibition in mice, a model for schizophrenia, without catalepsy, a common side effect of traditional antipsychotics.

candidates.title: Structural basis for cysteine-linked redox-state plasticity in mammalian methionine sulfoxide reductase A
candidates.authors: Shin B, Hawkes HJK, Park S, Ki H, Kim S, Shah F, Di Trapani G, Tonissen KF, Hwang KY
candidates.abstract: Methionine sulfoxide reductase A (MsrA) protects proteins from oxidative damage through cysteine-based redox cycling, but how mammalian MsrA is structurally regulated during oxidation and reductive recycling has remained unclear. We report three crystal structures of mouse MsrA (mMsrA) that capture distinct redox states — reduced (3.0 Å), BME-trapped intermediate-like (BTIL; 1.6 Å), and oxidized (1.9 Å) — and reveal an unrecognized layer of regulation centered on Cys107. The BTIL structure visualizes catalytic Cys72 as a mixed disulfide with β-mercaptoethanol (BME) alongside a sulfenic acid at Cys107, a configuration not previously observed. The oxidized structure resolves the canonical Cys72–Cys218 disulfide together with an unexpected Cys107–Cys227 pairing that locks a C-terminal loop into a cap over the active site. LC-MS/MS mapping, MD simulations, activity assays, and thioredoxin (Trx)-trapping experiments converge on a model in which Cys72 drives catalysis, while Cys107-mediated disulfide rearrangement and Cys227-directed Trx entry gate substrate access and enzymatic regeneration — defining a noncanonical oxidized state that expands the mechanistic repertoire of mammalian MsrA under oxidative stress.

candidates.title: Structural and functional insights into a Zn2+-transporting P-type ATPase
candidates.authors: Lyu P, Longhin E, Sabzian-Molaei F, Montalvillo Ortega F, Li P, Wang K, Duelli A, Al-Jubair T, Ahmed Hotiana H, Ramos Becares E, Croll T, Meloni G, Andersson M, Bågenholm V, Gourdon P
candidates.abstract: Zinc is essential for life yet toxic in excess, rendering homeostatic control vital for all organisms. Transition metal transporting P-type (PIB-) ATPase proteins are critical for this balance but remain poorly understood at the molecular level. Here, we present the inward-open structure of a dimeric zinc-transporting PIB-type ATPase, resolved at 3.6 Å resolution. Biochemical analyses and molecular dynamics simulations suggest that the N-terminal tail, harboring two so-called metal binding domains (MBDs), auto-inhibits the ATPase core and serves as a metal-sensitive sensor, releasing inhibition when intracellular metal levels rise. Contrary to the prevailing uptake models, the structure reveals an electronegatively charged uptake region that directly exposes a metal-binding cysteine of the invariant CPC-motif. We propose that a histidine-rich segment, positioned after the MBD closest to the core, donates ions to the CPC site. Consequently, an intricate interplay between the regulatory and ion-providing N-terminus and the ATPase core is present, safeguarding against zinc toxicity. Collectively, our findings shed light on the regulation and transport mechanism of PIB-ATPases, with implications for fundamental biology and the potential to inform future biotechnological and translational applications.

candidates.title: Syntaxin11 deficiency inhibits CRAC channel priming to suppress cytotoxicity and gene expression in T lymphocytes independent of membrane trafficking
candidates.authors: Datta S, Gupta A, Jagetiya KM, Bera R, Tiwari VR, Yamashita M, Yande AR, Rishad A, Malik V, Raran-Kurussi S, Ammann S, Shahrooei M, Mandal K, Sowdhamini R, Prakriya M, Dani A, Vig M
candidates.abstract: Mutations in Syntaxin11 (STX11), a Q-SNARE, result in a fatal immune disorder known as familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis 4 (FHLH4) in human patients. A key diagnostic feature of FHLH4 is defective T and natural killer cell cytotoxicity. Here, we show that STX11 directly binds and regulates Orai1, the pore-forming subunit of calcium release-activated calcium (CRAC) channels. CRAC channels enable store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) from the extracellular space and are crucial for granule exocytosis and nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT)-dependent gene expression in activated lymphocytes. STX11 depletion strongly inhibited SOCE, CRAC currents, NFAT activation, interleukin-2 gene expression, and degranulation in FHLH4 patient T lymphocytes and cell lines without affecting membrane trafficking. Remarkably, defects of cytolytic granule exocytosis, as well as interleukin-2 expression, could be reversed by ionomycin in patient T lymphocytes, and a constitutively active, H134S, mutant of Orai1 rescued calcium entry in STX11-depleted cells. Further analyses showed that STX11 ‘primes’ Orai1 for optimal on-site multimeric assembly, which was Stim independent but required for gating. Priming of ion channel pore subunits is, therefore, a primary function of specific SNAREs which may have preceded their role in membrane trafficking and vesicle fusion.

candidates.title: The mechanism of R2ab-mediated attachment to polystyrene surfaces in Staphylococcus epidermidis
candidates.authors: Yadav R, Perera YR, Somarathne RP, Shorie H, Carby S, Mishra A, Fitzkee NC
candidates.abstract: The staphylococcal autolysin protein hydrolyzes cell wall peptidoglycans. The R2ab repeats of autolysin guide the catalytic domain by binding to cell wall components and mediate attachment to abiotic surfaces during biofilm formation on polystyrene. Characterizing protein interactions with surfaces is a significant challenge in understanding bacterial attachment. Here, using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, we determined the solution structure and backbone dynamics of the R2ab domain. We then, by combining nuclear magnetic resonance and calorimetry, identified the interaction mode of R2ab with cell wall components and polystyrene surfaces. The solution-derived R2ab structure reveals interaction surfaces with lipoteichoic acid and peptidoglycan. The binding regions are identified, and docking is used to model their binding to R2ab. R2ab also interacts with polystyrene nanoparticles. Using a novel approach where polystyrene nanoparticles are paramagnetically labeled, we identify the major R2ab-polystyrene interaction interface. R2ab engages polystyrene surfaces via a defined C-terminal interface on R2b, as revealed by PRE mapping, isothermal titration calorimetry, and mutational analyses. Polar and charged residues (notably S776 and K779) play key roles in adsorption. These findings support a model in which R2ab acts as a molecular bridge, binding both cell wall components and abiotic surfaces. This highlights its role in early biofilm formation and suggests that disrupting this interaction could reduce Staphylococcus epidermidis attachment to abiotic surfaces.

candidates.title: AlphaDTA: integrating AlphaFold3 embeddings and 3D complex structures for drug–target binding affinity prediction
candidates.authors: Chung M, Park S, Lee H
candidates.abstract: Accurate prediction of drug–target binding affinity plays an important role in structure-based drug discovery, yet existing approaches are constrained by their reliance on scarce experimentally determined protein–ligand complex structures. In this context, recent advances in biomolecular structure prediction models, such as AlphaFold3, have emerged as a promising approach to alleviate the scarcity of experimentally determined protein–ligand complex structures. In this study, we introduce AlphaDTA, a framework that integrates AlphaFold3-predicted structures and embeddings for drug–target binding affinity prediction. AlphaDTA processes two types of AlphaFold3 embeddings, single and pair embeddings. We utilized the single embeddings at both fine-grained and coarse-grained levels to capture local interaction patterns and global binding context, and used the pair embeddings to encode cross-molecular relational features. The AlphaFold3-predicted structures are further processed by a three-dimensional structure-based geometric encoder to produce corresponding structural embedding representations. The resulting single, pair, and structural embeddings are then integrated through adaptive fusion for affinity prediction. When we evaluated AlphaDTA using recently proposed PDBbind data splits designed to reduce train–test structural overlap, AlphaDTA achieved state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multiple independent benchmarks. In a case study on the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator, AlphaDTA correctly identifies a clinically approved potentiator and suggests a potential repurposing candidate among FDA-approved drugs. Scientific contribution AlphaDTA enables accurate drug–target binding affinity prediction without relying on experimentally determined protein–ligand complex structures. By integrating AlphaFold3-derived single, pair, and structure-based embeddings through adaptive fusion, AlphaDTA improves generalization on structurally nonredundant benchmarks and demonstrates utility for target-specific drug repurposing.Graphical Abstract Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s13321-026-01259-6.

candidates.title: An artificial intelligence-assisted PARP-1-targeted PET imaging agent [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FZPF: From bench to clinic
candidates.authors: Ji M, Jiang C, Xi Y, Liu S, He S, Zhang J, Xu X, Yang Z, Wang X, Song S
candidates.abstract: Considering that clinical data for 68Ga-labeled poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP)-targeted probes have not yet been reported and integrated artificial intelligence (AI) workflows for radiotracer development are still lacking, to support radiotracer development and clinical translation, we constructed an AI-assisted multi-stage prioritization workflow and then synthesized two 68Ga-labeled PARP-1-targeted probes, validating their performance through in vitro, in vivo, and clinical evaluations. An AI-guided multi-objective workflow (encoder-decoder recurrent neural network (RNN) generation, convolutional neural network (CNN) docking scoring, Synthetic Complexity Learned from a Reaction Corpus (SCScore)-based tractability triage, and deep neural network (DNN)) was used to prioritize a derivatization-ready Fuzuloparib analog (NH2-FZPF) and to guide chelator installation, yielding DOTA-FZPF and NOTA-FZPF precursors for subsequent 68Ga radiolabeling. Both [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FZPF and [68Ga]Ga-NOTA-FZPF exhibited high radiochemical purity, stability, and PARP-1-targeted specificity. In tumor models, [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FZPF displayed favorable tumor uptake and rapid background clearance, supporting further evaluation. Exploratory positron emission tomography (PET) assessments of Fuzuloparib target engagement show the specificity and functionality of [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FZPF, supporting in vivo evaluation of PARP inhibitor target engagement and pharmacodynamics. This study recruited 4 cancer patients and performed positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scans using [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FZPF. Biopsy specimens showed that PET/CT-positive lesions corresponded to regions of high PARP-1 expression. This study demonstrates how an AI rational design workflow can support decision-making in radiotracer design while maintaining synthetic feasibility and translational potential. These preliminary findings support the clinical feasibility of [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FZPF and suggest that it is promising for non-invasive assessment of PARP-1 expression and dynamic monitoring of in vivo target occupancy and pharmacodynamics.

candidates.title: Biofabricated Al2O3 nanoparticles as a recyclable heterogeneous catalyst for nicotinonitrile synthesis: antimicrobial activity, molecular docking and ADMET assessment
candidates.authors: Kokare P, More A, Pandit N, Ghanwat V, Jadhav A, Sawant A, Bagade C, mali D, Mahanwar S, Kamble S
candidates.abstract: An efficient and environmentally benign Al2O3 nanoparticle-catalyzed protocol was developed for the synthesis of nicotinonitrile derivatives under mild reaction conditions using an ethanol–water solvent system. The Al2O3 nanoparticles were synthesized via a green approach employing Coccinia indica leaf extract and characterized by XRD, SEM, EDS, FTIR, and BET analyses. The developed catalytic protocol afforded excellent yields (88–96%) within short reaction times (18–40 min), demonstrating a broad substrate scope, high catalytic activity, and excellent recyclability. The synthesized nicotinonitrile derivatives were further evaluated for their antimicrobial activity against S. aureus, B. subtilis, P. aeruginosa, and E. coli, exhibiting promising antibacterial efficacy. Molecular docking studies against the bacterial DNA gyrase B enzyme further supported their potential antimicrobial mechanism, while in silico ADMET analysis indicated favorable drug-likeness and toxicity profiles. Overall, this study demonstrates a sustainable nanocatalytic strategy for the efficient synthesis of biologically active nicotinonitrile derivatives.

candidates.title: BiotaPredictor: A machine learning framework for predicting drug depletion by the human gut microbiota
candidates.authors: Naranjani B, McCoubrey LE, Borde A, Hulthe G, Josefson M, Abrahmsén-Alami S, Abrahamsson B, Basit AW
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTThe gut microbiota can profoundly influence the performance of oral medicines by metabolizing or bioaccumulating drugs, thereby reducing systemic exposure and contributing to variable patient responses. Despite growing recognition of these interactions, microbiota-driven drug depletion remains insufficiently addressed during early development. Here, we present BiotaPredictor, a freely accessible web-based machine learning platform that predicts the likelihood of drug depletion by human intestinal microbiota from molecular structure. We compiled two curated datasets containing microbial depletion outcomes: (i) a consistently annotated AstraZeneca dataset (158 compounds) and (ii) an expanded integrated dataset incorporating published evidence (522 compounds). Multiple molecular descriptors—including physicochemical properties, 3D conformational features, and fingerprint-based encodings—were evaluated across a suite of classification algorithms. A logistic regression model trained on the AstraZeneca dataset using physicochemical parameters achieved the highest performance, correctly classifying all compounds in an external validation study (3 depleted, 9 stable). BiotaPredictor enables early triage of compounds susceptible to microbiota-mediated loss and can inform lead optimization, formulation strategy, and pharmacokinetic prediction. Integrating microbiota liability assessment into development pipelines will contribute to safer, more efficacious drug products and support precision delivery of orally administered therapeutics.

candidates.title: Comparative biochemical analysis of tea (Camellia sinensis) and coffee (Coffea arabica) extracts identifies the ethyl acetate fraction of green tea as a potential dual digestive enzyme inhibitor: an in vitro and in silico study
candidates.authors: El-Saied YE, Elgazar AA, El-Senduny FF, Hammouda NE, El-Khawaga OY, Badria FA
candidates.abstract: Metabolic diseases, including obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), have prompted interest in identifying natural products capable of modulating digestive enzymes. This study comparatively evaluated the phytochemical composition, antioxidant activity, and digestive enzyme inhibitory activities of green tea (GT), black tea (BT), and green coffee (GC) extracts. Phytochemical screening, antioxidant assays (DPPH, ABTS, and SOD-like), and quantitative phenolic analysis indicated that GT contained the highest phenolic content and exhibited the greatest antioxidant activity, whereas GC showed the highest alkaloid content. Among the fractionated extracts, the ethyl acetate fraction of green tea (EtOAc fraction of GT) was selected for further investigation based on its phenolic content, pancreatic lipase inhibitory activity, and overall biological profile. HPLC analysis identified ferulic acid and chlorogenic acid as major constituents, together with syringic acid, resveratrol, myricetin, and rosmarinic acid. Both the crude BT extract and EtOAc fraction of GT exhibited α-amylase inhibitory activity comparable to that of quercetin. Kinetic analysis indicated competitive inhibition by the EtOAc fraction of GT (IC50 = 0.662 mg mL−1), whereas BT displayed mixed-type inhibition with a strong uncompetitive component. The EtOAc fraction of GT also showed the lowest IC50 against pancreatic lipase (0.264 mg mL−1) and followed a non-competitive inhibition mechanism. The EtOAc fraction maintained 98.94% of human skin fibroblast viability after 48 h at 500 µg mL−1 in a preliminary cytotoxicity screen. Molecular docking was consistent with the experimental findings, suggesting that hesperidin and rutin may contribute to competitive α-amylase inhibition and allosteric pancreatic lipase modulation. These findings indicate that the ethyl acetate fraction of green tea is a phenolic-rich fraction with dual digestive enzyme inhibitory activity that merits further evaluation in appropriate biological models.

candidates.title: Decoding channel pore dynamics mechanism in Anopheles gambiae Orco homotetramer
candidates.authors: Chidambara Thanu V, Jabeen A, Kythreoti G, Iatrou K, Zographos SE, Taylor PW, Ranganathan S
candidates.abstract: AbstractMotivationInsect odorant receptors (iORs) essential for olfaction function as 7-transmembrane-domain (7TM) ion channels. iORs form tetrameric complexes that include a highly conserved odorant receptor co-receptor (Orco). Functional Orco homotetramers have also known to form ex vivo. Blocking Orco ex vivo and in vivo disrupts olfactory signalling, making it a promising target for functional intervention. Understanding its gating behaviour is critical for developing strategies to disrupt odour-guided behaviours in disease-vector insects. Thus, insights into the dynamic gating of the Anopheles gambiae Orco have implications on the rational design of vector-control strategies against malaria. We studied molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on homotetrameric AgamOrco models generated using template-based modelling (TBM) and AlphaFold3 (AF3), to investigate ligand-dependent pore dynamics. Agonist and antagonist bound systems were analysed to understand the ligand-dependent gating.ResultsOur results show that apo and antagonistic IPC-bound AgamOrco homotetramer models remain in a stable, closed, and non-conductive state across both models. TBM, but not AF3, successfully captures agonistic VUAA1-induced activation, consistent with experimental observations, exhibiting asymmetric pore widening and conformational changes. Antagonist displacement simulations confirm IPC-mediated pore closure. Overall, the TBM AgamOrco model provides a reliable framework for structure-guided discovery of novel agents for control of insect pests and vector diseases.

candidates.title: Design, synthesis, and anticancer evaluation of Biginelli-derived DHPM–amide hybrids bearing clinically inspired kinase-directed pharmacophores: EGFR docking and DFT studies
candidates.authors: Kothadiya SP, Maheta JB, Lakhnotra DK, Bhola YO, Koradiya SB
candidates.abstract: A series of twelve novel dihydropyrimidine (DHPM)–amide hybrid conjugates (6a–c, 8a–c, 10a–c, and 12a–c) were rationally designed, synthesized, and biologically evaluated as potential EGFR-targeted anticancer agents against A549 non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) cells. The target compounds were constructed via a convergent two-step protocol: Biginelli multicomponent condensation to assemble the DHPM–carboxylic acid core (4a–c), followed by EDC·HCl/HOBt-mediated chemoselective amide coupling with four clinically inspired amine fragments derived from erlotinib/gefitinib (series 10), cabozantinib (series 8), imatinib (series 12), and a sorafenib bioisostere (series 6). All compounds were characterized by IR, 1H NMR, 13C NMR, and low-resolution ESI-MS. MTT cytotoxicity screening identified compound 10b as the most potent analogue (IC50 = 16.11 ± 0.11 µg mL−1, equivalent to 23.31 µM), exceeding the molar potency of the reference methotrexate (IC50 = 15.00 ± 0.48 µg mL−1, equivalent to 33.01 µM). It should be noted that methotrexate is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor included solely as a general cytotoxicity control and is not a mechanistically matched EGFR comparator; the comparison therefore reflects relative cytotoxic potency only and does not imply EGFR selectivity. Molecular docking against EGFR (PDB 1M17), an erlotinib-bound inactive-conformation structure, returned the most favourable score for 10b (score = −7.819 kcal mol−1), with predicted hydrogen bonds to ASP831 and LYS721, a halogen contact at ILE765, and an extensive 15-residue hydrophobic network; these poses indicate compatibility with the erlotinib-binding pocket rather than a confirmed ATP-competitive binding mode. DFT calculations at B3LYP/6-311G(d,p) characterised the electronic structure of the isolated molecule (ΔE = 4.045 eV; ω = 3.155 eV) and are reported as a physicochemical description only, without implying a causal link to cellular activity. Normal mode analysis indicated conformational stability of the 10b–EGFR complex, collectively identifying 10b as a promising lead for further optimisation and mechanistic evaluation, for which direct EGFR kinase assays remain necessary.

candidates.title: Evaluating Machine Learning Affinity Prediction Methods on Novel Lead Optimization Data: A 15‐PGDH Case Study
candidates.authors: Rich AS, Dodda LS, Price DJ
candidates.abstract: Recent machine learning (ML) methods for protein–ligand affinity prediction, such as Boltz‐2 and AEV‐PLIG, have been reported to approach free energy perturbation (FEP) accuracy on well‐known benchmarks. Even short of that accuracy, ML‐based potency models that fall between FEP and common docking scoring functions in accuracy and speed offer clear potential value. Here, we report a case study using recently disclosed data from four related ligand series targeting 15‐hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase (15‐PGDH). We evaluate each ML method's predictive accuracy with a focus on when it could be used to influence synthetic priorities. AEV‐PLIG performed poorly across most series, and adding literature 15‐PGDH inhibitors to its training did not improve performance. Boltz‐2 performed well on series most similar to published inhibitors in its training, achieving accurate cofolding (median ligand RMSD ≤0.81 Å) and rank order. However, for a series exploring a new region of the binding pocket, Boltz‐2 sometimes generated less accurate poses and predicted all ligands in the series to be less potent than a published exemplar, despite experimental potency gains of up to 500x. These results highlight both the promise in well‐characterized chemical space and limitations in the novel regions where computational guidance is most needed.

candidates.title: Exploring the bistable equilibrium of methylated CpG DNA recognition by the MBD2 protein
candidates.authors: Volkenandt S, Belyaeva J, Li T, Elgeti M, Metzler R, Imhof P, Williams DC, Bagherpoor Helabad M
candidates.abstract: AbstractMethyl-CpG binding domain 2 (MBD2) is a critical epigenetic regulator that selectively binds methylated CpG dinucleotides, key marks controlling gene regulation and chromatin organization. Understanding the interactions and conformational dynamics underlying this high selectivity is essential to elucidate MBD2’s regulatory role. Here, using extensive classical MD simulations, we explored the formation of the MBD2–mCpG recognition complex. By initially positioning MBD2 one base pair downstream of its target, we observed its transition to the target site within microseconds. Notably, upon binding, MBD2 adopts two distinct stable conformations: a primary state closely resembling the X-ray crystal structure, and a secondary state of reduced affinity that nevertheless retains comparable selectivity for mCpG. Our results establish S189 as a key macro-switch; loss of its interaction with the methylcytosine backbone shifts the equilibrium toward the secondary state. This is corroborated by MD simulations of the S189A mutant, which preferentially adopts the secondary state-like conformation. Complementary NMR experiments confirm that S189A mutation does not alter mCpG selectivity, while fluorescence polarization measurements reveal a reduced binding affinity, consistent with our MD simulations results. Together, these findings indicate that MBD2 binding to methylated CpG involves a bistable equilibrium, providing new insights into how high affinity and adaptability are balanced in epigenetic recognition. In a broader context, our findings suggest that such alternative bound-state equilibria may represent an inherent feature of specific protein–DNA complexes.

candidates.title: Glis1 regulates metabolic programming by promoting H3K18 lactylation to alleviate neuronal senescence following spinal cord injury
candidates.authors: Li D, Lu X, Gong Z, Wu J, Zhang Y, Wu J, Xu C, Guo X, Xu G, Xu H, Yang S, Xia X, Lu F, Jiang J, Lu S, Sheng J, Ma X, Zhu W, Zou F, Sun C, Gu X, Guan Y
candidates.abstract: Neuronal senescence is a significant factor impeding spinal cord injury (SCI) repair. Research indicates that Glis1, a Kruppel-like zinc finger transcription factor, is pivotal in reprogramming senescent cells and enhancing genomic stability via lactylation. Histone lactylation, an epigenetic modification using lactate as a substrate, becomes prominent post-SCI due to increased neuronal lactate levels. However, the mechanisms linking neuronal senescence and histone lactylation following SCI remain poorly understood. This study elucidates the roles of Glis1, H3K18 lactylation, and neuronal senescence through comprehensive in vivo and in vitro investigations. The findings reveal a post-SCI rise in neuronal lactate levels, accompanied by cellular senescence. Furthermore, upregulation of Glis1 attenuates senescence and promotes histone lactylation. The downstream target secretogranin II (SCG2), identified via ChIP-seq and RNA-seq, was found to exert negative feedback on glycolytic metabolism and lactylation, thereby suppressing neuronal senescence. These results unveil a novel regulatory mechanism of Glis1 in neuronal senescence following SCI through the p300/H3K18la/SCG2 axis, offering a new therapeutic target for spinal cord repair.

candidates.title: Global resurgence of norovirus GII.17[P17] accompanies shifting phylogeographic connectivity patterns: surveillance in Jiangsu, 2023–2025
candidates.authors: Li C, Xiao J, Ai J, Qin Y, Xu K, Zhu L, Wang S, Fu J
candidates.abstract: BackgroundNorovirus GII.17[P17] has re-emerged and has been circulating globally since 2023. In Jiangsu, China, we found that its proportion increased from 2024 onward. Using local surveillance data combined with global sequences, we reconstructed the global spatiotemporal dynamics of GII.17[P17] and explored its evolution and molecular mechanisms.MethodsSamples were subjected to whole-genome sequencing using next-generation sequencing. We used bioinformatics tools to analyze the full viral protein 1 sequences for molecular evolution, spatiotemporal phylogeographic associations, and amino acid changes.ResultsFrom October 2024 to May 2025, 209 GII.17[P17] outbreaks were reported (approximately 26 per month), while only 23 outbreaks occurred in the full year of 2023 (fewer than 2 per month). In sporadic case surveillance, the proportion of GII.17[P17] increased from 9.6% in 2023 to 62.4% in January–May 2025. The maximum clade credibility tree showed that GII.17[P17] clustered into two large clusters. Most samples from 2024 to 2025 belonged to Lineage 3 of Cluster II. In the phylogenetic network and minimum spanning tree, we identified three core hub strains. Inferred phylogeographic connectivity patterns suggest a shift in the primary centers of viral lineage dispersal from East Asia (Cluster I, 2014–2016) to Northwest Europe (Cluster II, 2021–2025). Molecular evolutionary analysis revealed that the current dominant lineage (Lineage 3, Cluster II) exhibited an evolutionary rate of 4.126 × 10−3 substitutions/site/year (95% HPD: 3.27–4.98 × 10−3), substantially higher than the earlier Cluster I lineages (1.798 × 10−3; 95% HPD: 1.41–2.19 × 10−3; posterior probability >0.99; 95% HPD intervals non-overlapping).ConclusionInferred phylogeographic connectivity patterns indicate that the primary centers of GII.17[P17] lineage dispersal have shifted from East Asia (2014–2016) to Northwest Europe (2021–2025). The current dominant lineage (Lineage 3, Cluster II) exhibits an accelerated evolutionary rate, approximately 2.3-fold faster than Cluster I lineages, and carries lineage-specific amino acid substitutions in antigenic epitopes temporally associated with its global expansion. These findings highlight the value of sustained genomic surveillance in regions with high inferred phylogeographic connectivity for monitoring norovirus evolution.

candidates.title: Gαo/z-biased coupling profile of the dopamine D3 receptor
candidates.authors: Zanetti L, Franchini L, Saha S, Liao Y, Muntean BS, Orlandi C
candidates.abstract: Dopamine receptors are G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) that serve as key targets for FDA-approved drugs to treat various neuropsychiatric disorders. Notably, ~11% of all marketed GPCR-targeting drugs act on dopamine receptors. Five GPCRs mediate the effects of endogenous dopamine and compounds used to treat Parkinson’s disease, schizophrenia, and other conditions. However, on-target side effects associated with these medications highlight the need to analyze dopamine receptor signaling to design safer, more effective therapeutics. Here, we characterize the G protein coupling of dopamine D2-like receptors and observe the striking inability of D3R to engage with Gαi proteins while effectively activating Gαo/z subtypes. Applying orthogonal cell-based assays with wild-type G proteins in parental and ΔGαi/o/z cells, we conclusively establish that D3R does not activate Gαi proteins. Further analysis of Gαi2:GαoA and D2R:D3R chimeras reveals that this selective inability is driven by molecular determinants located within the α5 helix of Gαi and ICL2 of D3R. Guided by cryo-EM structures, we model the interface between these regions to clarify the structural basis of selectivity. Finally, treating hippocampal neurons in acute slices with selective agonists and antagonists reveals marked differences in their regulation of endogenous adenylyl cyclase and cAMP, underscoring the neurophysiological significance of our findings.

candidates.title: How a Highly Acidic SH3 Domain Binds to Its Intrinsically Disordered Partner through the Formation of an Encounter Complex Intermediate
candidates.journal: The Journal of Physical Chemistry. B
candidates.authors: Jaramillo-Martinez V, Kukreja R, Cohen MR, Mujica A, Barton S, Onwuzulu OC, Cardoso J, Dominguez MJ, Kekwick IM, Ali J, Bell GM, Rice S, Poaquiza D, McClure C, Anguiano F, Latham MP, Ball KA, Stollar EJ
candidates.abstract: Electrostatic interactions often play a role in determining the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of protein–protein interactions. However, the role of long-range electrostatic interactions in intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) binding is less clear, as they often bind in multiple steps, including initial formation of a disordered encounter complex, followed by rearrangement into the bound state. We varied the salt concentration to probe the role of long-range electrostatic interactions in the binding of the highly charged AbpSH3 domain and the oppositely charged IDP ArkA. Using isothermal titration calorimetry, we observed that salt enthalpically destabilizes the bound complex. Molecular dynamics and NMR experiments revealed that salt has little effect on the bound state structure. However, simulations show that salt destabilizes the encounter complex intermediate, which primarily affects the association rate as measured by NMR. Consistent with these results, salt has the largest stabilizing effect on the apo SH3 domain, as cations substitute for the transient and long-range electrostatic interactions that can form with ArkA in the complex. We revealed a detailed picture of how a highly charged domain uses long-range, fuzzy, electrostatic interactions to help reach the bound state, a mechanism that is likely common among other highly charged domains that bind IDPs.

candidates.authors: Zhang A, Chen H, Song N, Zhuang J, Chen B, Lin X, Jin S, Chen C
candidates.abstract: Knee trauma is an important risk factor for post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA), a progressive joint disease characterized by articular cartilage degeneration and limited disease-modifying treatment options. Matrix metalloproteinase-13 (MMP-13/collagenase-3) contributes to cartilage extracellular matrix degradation through cleavage of type II collagen, making it a relevant molecular target for cartilage-protective drug discovery. This study aimed to identify and prioritize potential small-molecule MMP-13 inhibitors using an integrated in silico workflow. The workflow included MMP-13 sequence retrieval, structural characterization, pharmacophore-based screening, molecular docking, ADMET/toxicity prediction, protein-ligand interaction analysis, protein-protein interaction and co-expression network analysis, and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation. Among the screened compounds, P4C-BM was prioritized as an early-stage computational lead candidate based on its combined docking score, predicted ADMET profile, interaction pattern, and molecular dynamics stability. However, the findings are preliminary and computational only. The present study does not experimentally demonstrate direct MMP-13 inhibition, selectivity against other MMP family members, cartilage repair, clinical efficacy, or synergy with platelet-rich plasma, physiotherapy, or other treatment modalities. Among the screened compounds, P4C-BM was prioritized as an early-stage computational lead candidate based on its combined docking score, predicted ADMET profile, interaction pattern, and molecular dynamics stability. However, the findings are preliminary and computational only. The present study does not experimentally demonstrate direct MMP-13 inhibition, selectivity against other MMP family members, cartilage protection, cartilage repair, disease modification, or clinical efficacy. Therefore, P4C-BM should be regarded only as a candidate for further experimental validation in enzymatic assays, chondrocyte models, cartilage explant studies, and in vivo osteoarthritis or post-traumatic osteoarthritis models. candidates.authors: Abbas N, Arfan M, Iqbal Y, Iqbal M, Ahmed N, Alharbi MG, Gatasheh MK
candidates.abstract: This study reports the synthesis of neurotransmitter-inspired, biolabile mononuclear Mg(ii)/(NY1) and Ca(ii)/(NY2) metallocarboxylates of N-phthaloyl-γ-aminobutyric acid ligand (NPGABA), motivated by the growing relevance of metallocarboxylates in addressing essential metal-ion deficiencies. Extensive spectral (i.e. IR, UV-vis, 1H-NMR, 13C-NMR, AAS, and ICP-AES) and analytical (SEM, micro-analysis and thermal gravimetric analysis) techniques were used to characterize and confirm the formation of the ligand and its metal carboxylate complexes. The complexes were confirmed to have the formulas [Mg(NPGABA)2(H2O)2]4 (NY1) and [Mg(NPGABA)2(H2O)4] (NY2), where NPGABA is the abbreviation of the ligand in its deprotonated form. The DNA-binding interactions of the NPGABA ligand (NY0) and its alkaline earth metal carboxylate complexes with magnesium (Mg/NY1) and calcium (Ca/NY2) were investigated through a combination of biophysical, computational, and biological assays. UV-visible absorption studies revealed a significant hyperchromic effect without a bathochromic/hypsochromic shift, indicative of a non-intercalative external binding mode (i.e., minor groove binding or electrostatic interaction with the anionic sugar phosphate backbone of DNA). Binding constants (Kb) were calculated by UV-vis spectroscopy at a temperature of 310.15 K and pH of 7.4 as 2.18 × 105 M−1 (NY0), 4.05 × 105 M−1 (NY1), and 4.21 × 105 M−1 (NY2), with Gibbs free energies (ΔG°) of −31.68, −33.28, and −33.38 kJ mol−1, respectively, confirming spontaneous interactions. Similarly, fluorescence emission spectroscopic studies demonstrated eminent quenching without any shift, providing complementary evidence for the presence of external non-intercalative interactions. Accordingly, the binding constants (Kb) calculated by this technique under the same physiological conditions were 1.2 × 104 M−1 (NY0), 4.41 × 104 M−1 (NY1), and 8.61 × 104 M−1 (NY2), with binding site numbers of 0.86 (NY0), 0.95 (NY1), and 1.01 (NY2) and Gibbs free energies (ΔG°) of −24.23, −27.56, and −29.27 kJ mol−1, respectively, confirming the spontaneity of the interaction process. Molecular docking simulations against the canonical B-DNA (PDB: 1BNA) and the aromatase cytochrome P450 enzyme (PDB: 3EQM) also supported the occurrence of non-intercalative external binding interactions, with NY2 demonstrating the most favorable binding pose and energy. This non-intercalative external binding interaction was further endorsed by minute perturbation in the DNA solution viscosity and analogical consistency with classical groove binders like netropsin and distamycin A (Kb ≈ 105–107 M−1). The observed DNA binding affinity trend (NY2 > NY1 > NY0) has a direct correlation with the cytotoxic potency of the investigated compounds against triple negative breast cancer cells (MDA-MB-231). This consolidated investigation proved NY2 as a non-intercalative DNA-binding small molecule with preliminary anticancer activity, offering a strategic route for developing sustainable metallocarboxylate-based therapeutics.

candidates.authors: Wu YW, Yang CL, Fang-Chin YT, Yeh YH, Chen BJ, Sung TY, Chu JC, Lin TE, Yen SC, Hsieh JH, Huang SH, Chu CY, Yang KC, Hsu KC, Pan SL
candidates.abstract: AbstractPancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a lethal malignancy with limited targeted therapeutic options. Mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase kinase 4 (MAP4K4) has been implicated in PDAC progression, but the development of effective MAP4K4 inhibitors requires further improvement in potency, selectivity, and mechanistic characterisation. We previously identified F389-0746 as a selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor with anti-cancer activity in pancreatic cancer. Here, we used the F389-0746 scaffold to guide the selection and evaluation of benzoxazine-based analogs, followed by biochemical, structural, selectivity, and cellular characterisation of the most potent analogue. Among the identified analogs, F389-0736 showed the strongest MAP4K4 inhibitory activity, with an IC50 value of 44.0 nM, representing an approximately threefold improvement over F389-0746. Docking and structure-activity relationship analyses identified key binding interactions that support the enhanced potency of F389-0736 within the MAP4K4 binding pocket. Kinase profiling further demonstrated the selectivity of F389-0736 for MAP4K4 across the tested kinase panel. CETSA further demonstrated F389-0736-induced thermal stabilisation of MAP4K4, supporting intracellular target engagement. In pancreatic cancer cells, F389-0736 suppressed TAK1, JNK, and p38 phosphorylation and significantly reduced cell viability and proliferation, with IC50 and GI50 values of 4.41–4.65 μM and 4.03–5.12 μM, respectively. F389-0736 also inhibited clonogenic growth and induced sub-G1 accumulation with activation of apoptotic signalling. RNA sequencing identified 398 differentially expressed genes and revealed enrichment of inflammatory and stress response pathways, programmed cell death programs, oncogenic signalling perturbation, and metabolic reprogramming. These findings identify F389-0736 as a potent and selective benzoxazine-based MAP4K4 inhibitor and support its use as a chemical probe and lead scaffold for investigating MAP4K4-dependent signalling and therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer.

candidates.title: Overlapping RAD18-and DNA-binding interfaces in DNA polymerase η contribute to UV-induced DNA damage tolerance
candidates.authors: Kusumoto-Matsuo R, Masuda Y, Kanao R, Iwai S, Masutani C
candidates.abstract: DNA polymerase η (Polη) bypasses UV-induced pyrimidine dimers and thereby confers tolerance to UV irradiation. Although the C-terminus of Polη has been reported to interact with ubiquitinated PCNA and RAD18, how Polη engages RAD18 is not fully understood. Here, we show that Polη and RAD18 interact through two distinct modes in human cells: a ubiquitinated-PCNA-dependent mode that requires the Polη C-terminus, and an unexpected PCNA-independent mode mediated by its N-terminal region. We focused our subsequent analyses on this newly identified PCNA-independent mode. Using purified recombinant proteins, we demonstrate direct binding of the N-terminal region of human Polη (PolηΔC) to RAD18 in vitro. Although PolηΔC and RAD18 each bound primer-template DNA, we were unable to detect a ternary PolηΔC-RAD18-DNA complex, and DNA competitively inhibited RAD18 binding to both PolηΔC and full-length Polη. Mutational analyses revealed that the DNA-binding and RAD18-binding domains within Polη overlap. A separation-of-function mutant, PolηΔC(K317A), which retains near-normal DNA-binding and polymerase activities but exhibits reduced RAD18 binding in vitro, displayed a diminished ability to rescue the UV sensitivity of Polη-deficient cells. Notably, the detrimental impact of the K317A persisted in a PCNA-binding-defective background but was attenuated in RAD18-KO cells. These findings demonstrate that RAD18 binding to the N-terminal domain of Polη contributes to efficient bypass of pyrimidine dimers independently of the Polη-PCNA interaction and provide mechanistic insights into how Polη-RAD18 complexes assemble and dissociate during translesion DNA synthesis.

candidates.title: RCSB PDB web portal RCSB.org for biotechnology research: exploration and visualization of plastic-degrading enzymes at the atomic level in 3D
candidates.authors: Biester A, Zardecki C, Rose Y, Segura J, Duarte JM, Burley SK
candidates.abstract: IntroductionThe Research Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics Protein Data Bank (RCSB PDB) develops resources for biomolecular structure exploration and analysis that are used by an interdisciplinary community of bio scientists, researchers, and students numbering in the many millions worldwide. The RCSB.org website and suite of APIs provide access to more than 250,000 experimentally determined structures archived in the PDB, making it an invaluable tool for biotechnology, such as research on plastic-degrading enzymes. Engineering plastic-degrading enzymes represents a promising strategy for mitigating environmental accumulation of polyethylene terephthalate (PET).MethodsIn recent years, RCSB.org has provided access to more than 1 million Computed Structure Models (CSMs) alongside experimentally determined structures and introduced new tools for 3D Motif Search, Visualizing Sequence Annotations in 3D, and Pairwise Structure Alignment.Results and discussionTo identify site-directed mutagenesis targets for improving PET-degrading enzyme efficiency, biotechnology researchers utilize 3D structure data freely available from the PDB. This article describes how RCSB PDB tools for Advanced Search, Visualizing Sequence Annotations in 3D, and Pairwise Structure Alignment can be used to study plastic-degrading enzyme structure and function.

candidates.title: Repurposing amlodipine, fluoxetine, and escitalopram as non-antibiotic adjuvants: in vitro enhancement of ciprofloxacin and fluconazole activity against multidrug-resistant bacterial and candida clinical isolates
candidates.authors: Alkhawlani MA, Al-Madhagi WM, Alburyhi MM, Al-kaf AG, Al-Najar M
candidates.abstract: IntroductionMultidrug-resistant (MDR) Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Candida albicans threaten treatment success, particularly in resource-limited settings. Repurposing licensed, inexpensive non-antibiotic drugs may provide a strategy for enhancing the activity of established antimicrobial agents.MethodsClinical isolates from Sana’a, Yemen, and American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) reference strains were tested in vitro with amlodipine, fluoxetine, and escitalopram, individually and in dual or triple combinations with ciprofloxacin or fluconazole. Antimicrobial activity was evaluated using agar-well diffusion, broth microdilution minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), minimum bactericidal or fungicidal concentration (MBC/MFC), and checkerboard fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) assays. Molecular docking with AutoDock Vina was used to explore plausible interactions with MurB (PDB 1HSK), LasR (PDB 3IX3), and CYP51 (PDB 5V5Z). Normal mode analysis (NMA) with iMODS was performed for selected fluoxetine–LasR and fluoxetine–MurB complexes as a preliminary structural-dynamics assessment.ResultsFluoxetine produced inhibition zones of at least 27 mm across the tested organisms. Amlodipine produced larger zones against S. aureus and C. albicans than against P. aeruginosa, whereas escitalopram produced smaller zones overall. Checkerboard testing identified synergy (FICI ≤ 0.50) for selected combinations. Selected triple combinations reduced MIC values by 4- to 64-fold. The largest diffusion readouts were observed with ciprofloxacin + fluoxetine + amlodipine against S. aureus (101 mm), ciprofloxacin + fluoxetine + escitalopram against P. aeruginosa (88.5 mm), and ciprofloxacin + amlodipine + fluconazole against C. albicans (138.5 mm). Docking scores and NMA outputs provided hypothesis-generating structural context for the experimental findings.ConclusionsAntimicrobial enhancement was combination- and organism-dependent. Selected combinations showed checkerboard-defined synergy, whereas diffusion assays were interpreted as screening outcomes only. Docking and NMA findings were supportive and hypothesis-generating but did not establish target engagement or mechanism.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12866-026-05443-4.

candidates.title: Spins AfarLong-Range Pulse Dipolar EPR Spectroscopy Uncovers Curvature in TRIM25’s Coiled Coil
candidates.journal: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
candidates.authors: Limbach Y, Ackermann K, Chakraborty A, Norman DG, Bode BE
candidates.abstract: Pulse Dipolar Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (PDS) is a powerful method for determining nanometer distances in biomolecular systems. This methodology has been successfully used to validate structure hypotheses and to identify disorder. However, inherent distance limitations are under-explored. Many challenging biomolecular applications require long distance information, driving the need for a benchmarking study. We demonstrate distances up to 10.5 nm in TRIM25 reliably extracted from data obtained under standard sample conditions. By protein perdeuteration accurate distance measurements up to 17.3 nm were enabled. Enhancing sensitivity through optimization of the measurement and sample preparation conditions the achievable dipolar evolution time was extended to 150 μs. Thus, distances close to 20 nm should become experimentally accessible, highlighting the potential of advanced PDS methodologies for probing previously inaccessible long-range structural information in complex systems.

candidates.title: Targeting SLC1A5-mediated glutamine metabolism overcomes PARP inhibitor resistance in ovarian cancer
candidates.authors: Han F, Du H, Tian K, Qi G, Kong B, Luo X, Ma H
candidates.abstract: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi), such as olaparib, have significantly improved outcomes in ovarian cancer (OC); however, therapy resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Here, we showed that glutamine metabolism was upregulated in PARPi-resistant OC cells and identified the glutamine transporter SLC1A5 as a key mediator of this metabolic adaptation. Inhibition of SLC1A5 increased the sensitivity of OC cells to olaparib both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, we demonstrated that the deubiquitinating enzyme USP14 directly interacted with and stabilized SLC1A5 by removing K48-linked polyubiquitin chains, thereby enhancing glutamine uptake, promoting glutathione synthesis, alleviating oxidative stress, and activating the mTORC1 pathway. This metabolic rewiring improved DNA damage repair capacity and ultimately contributed to PARPi resistance. Notably, combined treatment with the SLC1A5 inhibitor V-9302 and olaparib synergistically suppressed tumor growth in a patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model. Collectively, our findings identify the USP14–SLC1A5 axis as a novel regulator of PARPi resistance and suggest that targeting glutamine metabolism represents a promising therapeutic strategy to overcome PARPi resistance in ovarian cancer.

candidates.abstract: Although cyclic SIAs have demonstrated promising medicinal potential, methodologies for their construction remain relatively scarce. SIAs have proven to be suitable nitrene precursors for aziridination and C–H amination, when mixed with hypervalent iodine and a metal catalyst. Herein, we report the intramolecular cyclization of SIAs featuring N-acyl-type substitution via a dirhodium nitrene intermediate, forming a new N-heteroatom bond. The reaction leads to a diverse array of aromatic heterocyclic products featuring stereogenic sulfur centers. A combination of computational and spectroscopic techniques were utilized to investigate the complex relationship between stereochemistry and aromaticity as well as to explore their unique electronic and geometric features. Finally, the potential for these heterocyclic motifs to be utilized for medicinal chemistry was evaluated by synthesizing an analogue of enzalutamide featuring the heterocyclic core and determining its resulting pharmacokinetic properties and bioactivity.

candidates.title: A Self-Regenerating Mixed-Valence FeOx-TiO2 Nanoplatform for Mitochondrion-Targeted Triple-Modal Cancer Therapy
candidates.authors: Xia Y, Wang M, Zhou Y, Wei R, Wang Y, Hua L, Fang Q, Chen Y
candidates.abstract: PurposeReactive oxygen species (ROS) cancer therapy is limited by short ROS lifetime, restricted diffusion, and lack of subcellular targeting. Current approaches physically mix independent components, causing complexity and decoupled actions. To overcome these barriers, we developed a mitochondrion-targeted nanoplatform (FTDT) built on a FeOₓ-TiO2 composite core with intrinsic mixed-valence Fe2⁺/Fe3⁺ pairs. The FT core acts as photosensitizer, while FeOₓ provides catalase- and peroxidase-like activities, integrating self-oxygenation, antioxidant depletion, self-amplifying redox cycling, photosensitization, photothermal conversion, and organelle anchoring into a single entity.MethodsFTDT was synthesized via a hydrothermal method, PDA coating, and TPP conjugation. Mixed-valence state was confirmed by XPS. Catalase- and peroxidase-like activities were evaluated by O2 and ∙OH detection. UV-Vis-NIR spectroscopy characterized optical absorption. Photothermal conversion was measured under 808 nm laser. 1O2 generation was detected using DPBF. Intracellular hypoxia, ROS, mitochondrial targeting, membrane potential, and lysosomal integrity were assessed by fluorescence microscopy. Cytotoxicity and in vivo efficacy were evaluated in A549 cells and xenograft mice.ResultsFTDT showed a self-amplifying cycle: Fe2⁺ drives ∙OH generation, Fe3⁺ consumes GSH and regenerates Fe2⁺; Fe3⁺ from Fenton reaction replenishes the Fe3⁺ pool. The core converted H2O2 to O2. FT core with PDA-enabled NIR absorption allowed 1O2 generation and photothermal conversion. TPP enabled mitochondrial localization, inducing dysfunction, lipid peroxidation, and lysosomal disruption, leading to cell death. In vitro and in vivo studies confirmed antitumor efficacy with good biocompatibility.ConclusionBy unifying self-oxygenation, antioxidant depletion, self-amplifying redox cycling, photosensitization, photothermal conversion, and organelle anchoring, FTDT offers a clinically translatable strategy to overcome key barriers in ROS-based cancer therapy.

candidates.title: A point mutation in duck plague virus gB enhances viral fusogenicity and intercellular dissemination via SNAP25-mediated membrane fusion
candidates.authors: Yang L, Du M, Jiang L, Cheng Z, Wen M, Wen G, Cheng A
candidates.abstract: Duck plague virus (DPV) is an alphaherpesvirus that causes significant economic losses to the poultry industry. Glycoprotein B (gB) is the core fusogen mediating membrane fusion during viral entry and cell-to-cell spread, yet the regulatory mechanisms governing gB-induced cell fusion in DPV remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified a single alanine-to-valine substitution at residue 942 of DPV gB (A942V) that unleashes the fusogenic potential of gB, leading to extensive syncytium formation in duck embryo fibroblasts. The A942V mutation significantly enhanced viral attachment, entry, and intercellular spread through fusion-mediated cytoplasmic channels, as revealed by transmission electron microscopy. In vivo, the mutant strain showed moderately increased pathogenicity—with survival rates of 60% versus 70% for the parental strain—without fundamentally altering the overall disease course. Proteomic profiling identified synaptosome-associated protein 25 (SNAP25) as a host factor markedly upregulated in DPV-A942V-infected cells. Mechanistically, the A942V mutation strengthened the binding affinity between gB and SNAP25, as corroborated by co-immunoprecipitation and molecular docking analyses (binding free energy: –82.92 kcal/mol; confidence score: 0.9478). Functional studies revealed that SNAP25 alone is sufficient to induce cell fusion, and that both its N- and C-terminal domains support fusion activity, whereas the middle region is functionally dispensable. SNAP25 overexpression enhanced, whereas knockdown reduced, viral proliferation and cell-to-cell spread without affecting viral attachment or entry. Collectively, these findings establish Ala942 of DPV gB as a critical inhibitory determinant of cell fusion and identify SNAP25 as a critical host dependency exploited by DPV to promote intercellular dissemination. Our study provides new insights into the molecular mechanisms of herpesvirus-induced cell fusion and highlights SNAP25 as a potential antiviral target for controlling DPV infection.

candidates.title: Akabane virus reprograms the PKR‑eIF2α‑SGs/PBs axis to fine-tune cap-snatching efficiency
candidates.authors: Liu Z, Chen D, Qin J, Wang J, Wang D, Ruan W, Xu S
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTAkabane virus (AKAV) initiates transcription in the cytoplasm via the cap-snatching mechanism. Cytoplasmic host mRNAs act as the primary cap donors, whereas the impact of their subcellular localization on the cap-snatching process remains unclear. Herein, we demonstrate that the AKAV-induced disassembly of polysomes, stress granules (SGs), and processing bodies (PBs) collectively facilitates viral cap-snatching. Mechanistically, AKAV infection activates the PKR-eIF2α signaling axis, leading to the disassembly of polysomes and subsequent translational shutoff. Intriguingly, the viral N protein disassembles SGs and PBs by competing for sequestered RNAs within these granules, whereas mutations of its RNA-binding residues abolish this activity. Moreover, PKR-eIF2α inhibition impairs AKAV replication and cap-snatching efficacy. In contrast, inhibition of SGs via G3BP1 knockdown or chemical agents significantly enhances viral replication and cap-snatching efficiency, indicating that polysomes and SGs disassembly favor caps acquisition. Additionally, N protein-mediated PBs disassembly protects mRNA from degradation, and PBs inhibition enhances cap-snatching. Taken together, AKAV has evolved a sophisticated strategy to reprogram mRNA distribution to create an optimal cellular environment for viral cap-snatching.

candidates.title: Automated Pharmacophore Hypothesis Generator for SILCS-Pharm: ph4gen
candidates.authors: Nordquist EB, MacKerell AD
candidates.abstract: Here we present ph4gen, a tool for the automated generation of pharmacophore hypotheses developed for use with the site identification by ligand competitive saturation (SILCS) technology. It builds upon the previously established SILCS-Pharm approach which generates the pharmacophore features from a given macromolecular structure, and SILCS-Hotspots which identifies potentially-druggable binding sites. The tool examines a set of pharmacophore features, typically 15–20, and ranks all permutations of hypotheses of a desired length, with default of 4 to 5 features per hypothesis. A diverse data set of seven proteins (namely, BACE1, CDK2, JNK1, P38, PTPT1B, Thrombin, and TYK2) and 336 ligands was used to train the logistic regression model which ranks these hypotheses and recalls at least one experimental pharmacophore hypothesis in four of seven cases in the top 10. The model was tested on a set of four separate proteins (namely FXR, HDM2, HSP90, and TRMD) and 354 ligands and recalls at least one experimental pharmacophore hypothesis in the top 5 in all four test systems, with mean precision and recall of 0.23±0.06 and 0.15±0.04, respectively. We show that the distribution of hypotheses generated is similar to that of the validated hypotheses, and that even in cases of near-misses, the pharmacophore hypotheses have similar chemical features to validated ones. The tool can also be tuned to provide greater or lesser chemical diversity when utilized in virtual screening. Ultimately, ph4gen is a useful tool as part of the SILCS workflow to identify druggable binding sites, generate drug-like pharmacophore hypotheses, and rank in silico hits for experimental validation.

candidates.title: Bruce suppresses autophagy-regulated caspase activity and wing tissue growth in Drosophila
candidates.authors: Shinoda N, Hama Y, Hanawa N, Miura M
candidates.abstract: Caspases are cysteine-aspartic proteases that mediate both lethal and non-lethal cellular outcomes, including the promotion of tissue growth. However, the mechanisms underlying the differential regulation of these activities remain unclear. We have previously shown that among the two Drosophila executioner caspases, Dcp-1 and Drice, Dcp-1 promotes tissue growth in a non-lethal manner, independent of canonical apoptotic signaling. Herein, we demonstrated that overexpressed Dcp-1, but not Drice, was activated without canonical apoptosome components. TurboID-based proximity labeling revealed distinct proximal proteomes, among which Sirtuin 1, an Atg8a deacetylase, which promotes autophagy, was specifically required for Dcp-1 activation. Autophagy-related genes, including Bcl-2 family members Debcl and Buffy, are required for Dcp-1 activation. Structure-based prediction using AlphaFold3 further identified Bruce, an autophagy-regulated inhibitor of apoptosis, as a Dcp-1-specific regulator acting outside the apoptosome-mediated pathway. Physiologically, Bruce suppresses wing tissue growth. These findings indicate that non-lethal Dcp-1 activity is governed by the autophagy–Bruce axis, enabling distinct non-lethal functions independent of cell death.

candidates.title: Cationized gelatin nanosphere-mediated release-controlled RNA interference targeting mTORC1 protects against intervertebral disc degeneration
candidates.authors: Hiranaka Y, Yurube T, Kumagai N, Takeoka Y, Kanda Y, Kuroshima K, Furuya M, Nakagawa D, Kitano T, Miyajima A, Washisaka T, Kakutani K, Kuroda R, Tabata Y
candidates.abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration is a major cause of chronic low back pain, but effective disease-modifying therapies remain unavailable. Sustained and localized RNA interference (RNAi) offers a promising therapeutic approach; however, its application to the disc is limited by poor local retention and delivery-related toxicity. Here, we developed a release-controlled RNAi platform using biodegradable cationized gelatin nanospheres (cGNS) to deliver small interfering RNA (siRNA) targeting Rptor, which encodes RPTOR, a key component of the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). cGNS enabled longer-term intracellular siRNA retention with lower toxicity than conventional lipofection, leading to a prolonged decrease in RPTOR expression, autophagy activation, and suppressed apoptosis, senescence, and matrix breakdown. Intradiscal delivery of Rptor siRNA with cGNS preserved radiographic tissue morphology, maintained histological matrix integrity, and reduced cellular degeneration markers. Benefits were observed in both preventive and post-traumatic settings. cGNS-mediated controlled release of RNAi against Rptor is a durable therapeutic strategy for degenerative disc disease through mTORC1 inhibition.

candidates.title: Comparative Toll-like receptor profiling reveals breed-specific innate immune architecture following Newcastle disease vaccination
candidates.authors: Nikunjkumar P, Kolluri G, Kaliappan A, Kurva SK, Vats A, Ramakrishnan S, Tyagi JS
candidates.abstract: The present study investigated the expression profiles of six TLR genes (TLR2A, TLR3, TLR4, TLR5, TLR7 and TLR21) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) following genotype II ND vaccination across fifteen genetically diverse chicken populations representing exotic, indigenous, fancy, synthetic and broiler parent lines. Relative gene expression was quantified by qPCR, and receptor expression data were integrated into five novel composite immune indices, namely the Viral Recognition Index (VRI), Bacterial Recognition Index (BRI), Immune Diversity Score (IDS), Shannon TLR Diversity Index (STDI), and Immune Breadth Index (IBI). Principal component analysis (PCA), hierarchical clustering and correlation analyses were further employed to characterize breed-specific innate immune architecture. Significant breed-dependent variation (P < 0.001) was observed for all six TLRs, demonstrating substantial genetic diversity in early pathogen recognition. Indigenous breeds, particularly Aseel Red and Kadaknath, exhibited broader activation of bacterial and viral recognition receptors, whereas White Frizzle showed the highest TLR2A expression and Frizzle displayed comparatively greater TLR5 and TLR7 expression among the fancy breeds. Synthetic populations exhibited intermediate but line-specific immune activation, while the broiler parent line (BCSFL) consistently demonstrated comparatively lower expression across most TLRs. PCA demonstrated pronounced breed-specific clustering of innate immune responses, with PC1 alone explaining 55.9% of the total variance, suggesting that coordinated TLR expression constituted the major source of immunological variation among chicken breeds. While correlation and hierarchical clustering analyses identified coordinated activation of bacterial (TLR2A, TLR4 and TLR5) and viral (TLR3, TLR7 and TLR21) sensing pathways in indigenous populations, whereas the Shannon TLR Diversity Index remained relatively conserved across most breeds. ND vaccine-induced TLR mediated immunity is characterized by functional specialization rather than hierarchical superiority, with distinct chicken genetic groups exhibiting differential investment in pathogen recognition pathways. The composite immune indices proposed herein provide a quantitative systems-level framework for evaluating innate immune architecture and represent promising hypothesis-generating biomarkers for comparative immunogenetics, precision breeding, and vaccine evaluation in poultry, warranting further validation through independent populations and virulent NDV challenge studies.

candidates.title: Constructing hypoxia and bioshield inhibits neurovascularized endochondral ossification for stable cartilage regeneration
candidates.authors: Tian Bx, Sun Hl, Bai Bs, Jin C, Wang Qy, Zhou Gd, Lin Xx, Wang B, Lei D, Hou Mj
candidates.abstract: Cartilage regeneration by bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) has become a promising therapeutic approach. However, the BMSC-engineered cartilage (BEC) is highly prone to ossification once implanted in vascularized and innervated subcutaneous microenvironments, ultimately leading to failure of cartilage regeneration. Herein, we innovatively developed a living cell-based encapsulation coating technique (designated as EC@GelMA) aimed at creating a biophysical barrier for BMSCs to maintain their stability in cartilage regeneration within an ectopic non-neurovascularized microenvironment. In vitro experimental results confirm that, both technically and theoretically, EC@GelMA could provide a hypoxic and biologically active biomimetic cartilage microenvironment for internally encapsulated BMSCs. In vivo experiments confirmed that EC@GelMA can provide BMSCs with a biomimetic cartilage microenvironment that isolates blood vessels and nerves, achieving stable cartilage regeneration of BMSCs in the ectopic microenvironment. All our results provide an effective solution for repairing cartilage defects in subcutaneous ectopic microenvironments, such as ear and nasal cartilage, using BMSCs, and facilitates its clinical translation.

candidates.title: Construction of electrostatic binding V-type starches using cationic starch and lauric acid: Insight into enhanced digestive resistance
candidates.authors: Ding Z, Li W, Xu C, Wang Y, Chen X
candidates.abstract: This study developed a V-type starch with enhanced structural stability and digestive resistance through an electrostatic interaction between a cationic starch (CS) and lauric acid (LA). X-ray diffraction analysis revealed that the non-etherified sample complexed with LA (ETA-0%-LA) exhibits a typical B-type crystalline structure. When the ETA content was increased from 5% to 30%, the V-type crystallinity of the CS–LA complexes increased from 9.22% to 24.60%. The degree of substitution (DS) exhibited a clear dose-dependent response to the etherifying agent, with ETA-30% yielding the highest DS (0.075%). Dynamic viscoelastic analysis further indicates that the electrostatic interaction between CS and LA substantially strengthened the gel network structure of CS–LA complexes. In vitro digestion tests confirmed that the moderate cationization markedly increasing resistant starch content and decreasing rapidly digestible starch content. These findings indicate that electrostatic interaction plays a key role in modulating the structural stability and digestive resistance of V-type starch.

candidates.title: Construction of multifunctional cerium-containing nanozyme hydrogel and its component-level functions in skin wound healing
candidates.authors: Bao X, Tang Q, Dong C, Xu M, Xu X
candidates.abstract: A multifunctional hydrogel composite incorporating cerium-based nanozymes is developed to modulate the wound microenvironment for skin regeneration. Cerium dioxide (CeO2) nanoparticles are surface-modified with hyperbranched poly-l-lysine (HBPL), which improves their dispersion and yields a hydrated particle size of approximately 304 nm. These nanozymes are combined with glycyrrhizic acid (GA) and gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) and crosslinked using visible light to form a CeO2-HBPL/GA/GelMA hydrogel. The resulting material exhibits tissue adhesion, skin-like mechanical properties, and an irregular porous architecture. In vitro, the hydrogel efficiently scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS), protects fibroblasts from oxidative damage, and inhibits Escherichia coli (E. coli) growth. It also promotes the polarization of macrophages from a pro-inflammatory (M1) to a pro-healing (M2) phenotype and enhances fibroblast proliferation. In a mouse full-thickness skin defect model, application of the hydrogel promotes wound closure, reduces scarring, and promotes complete epidermal regeneration. Histological analysis reveals decreased inflammatory infiltration and dense, organized collagen deposition resembling healthy skin. This multifunctional dressing integrates antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial activities, providing a proof-of-concept strategy for acute cutaneous wound repair.
